sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Central Tendency Breakdown Studio! Drag the contamination slider to inject gross leverage outliers into our Gaussian distribution. Observe how the arithmetic mean collapses immediately at 5%, the 20% trimmed mean breaks at 20%, Hodges-Lehmann survives to 29.3%, and the median resists all the way to 50%!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the simulator needles, Nova! As I push outliers to 25%, the mean is wrecked and the trimmed mean fails, but Hodges-Lehmann and median are still holding completely firm!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1: A survey records customer feedback on a 5-point Likert scale, and an engineer reports an arithmetic mean of 3.64. Why does this violate Stevens' measurement invariance theorem, and what is the methodologically sound alternative? Select Option A, B, or C above me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: A 5-point Likert scale and an arithmetic mean of 3.64! Review our three options above me and select the correct mathematical critique!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Correct! Likert ratings are purely Ordinal. Distances between categories are non-metric, and arbitrary monotonic relabelings preserve order but alter mean rankings across groups. The admissible metrics are the Median, Interquartile Range, and cumulative ordinal logistic models.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. Likert ratings are not Interval or Ratio variables because perceptual spacing between categories is subjective and non-constant. An arbitrary monotonic transformation like 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 changes the arithmetic mean order. You must report median and interquartile range.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Pipeline Throughput Workbench! Adjust Stage A and Stage B processing rates using the sliders. Watch how the arithmetic mean gives a false, optimistic rate, while the harmonic mean predicts the exact physical runtime down to the second, exposing an 80% latency budgeting gap!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at that Jensen gap, Nova! When Stage A runs at 100 requests per second and Stage B runs at 20, the arithmetic mean predicts 3,333 seconds, but the true runtime is 6,000 seconds! The harmonic mean matches physical reality perfectly!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2: In a two-stage pipeline processing 100,000 items per stage, Stage 1 processes at 100 requests per second and Stage 2 processes at 20 requests per second. A manager calculates the average throughput as 60 requests per second and budgets 3,333 seconds. What is the fundamental physical flaw? Select Option A, B, or C above me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: One hundred requests per second followed by twenty requests per second! Review our three options above me and select the correct physical analysis!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding! Throughput is work divided by elapsed time. Because Stage 2 is slower, the pipeline spends 5,000 seconds in Stage 2 and only 1,000 seconds in Stage 1. This 5-to-1 time-weighting forces overall throughput to follow the Harmonic Mean of 33.33 requests per second, taking 6,000 seconds total—an 80% delay over the false arithmetic budget!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. The arithmetic mean of rates assumes equal time is spent at each speed. Because items spend 5 times longer in the 20 req/s stage than in the 100 req/s stage, elapsed time accumulates inversely with rate, making the true physical throughput strictly the Harmonic Mean.
